opus-5.5.text:
The thing that worries me most is that language has become a kind of crutch. Right now most multimodal systems are really language models with eyes bolted on. You take a vision encoder, project its features into the token space of an LLM, and then the language model does all the "thinking." It works surprisingly well on benchmarks, but I think it hides a deep problem: the visual representation is being shaped to serve language, rather than to understand the world.

Language is an incredibly compressed, lossy description of reality. When we say "a cup on the table," we've thrown away almost everything: the geometry, the physics, the lighting, how the cup would fall if you pushed it. Humans can afford that compression because we already have a rich, grounded world model underneath. We learned to see, to move, to predict long before we learned to talk. Animals have very sophisticated visual intelligence with no language at all. So if we build AI the other way around, language first and perception as an afterthought, I'm not sure we ever recover that grounding.

There's also a practical symptom. A lot of current multimodal models can answer questions about an image without really looking at it. They rely on language priors. If you probe carefully, with spatial reasoning, counting, or fine-grained correspondence, they fail in ways that are almost embarrassing. That tells me the visual side hasn't learned a strong enough representation; it's leaning on the text.

And I worry about the research culture this creates. Because language models are so powerful, there's a temptation to evaluate everything through language, to treat vision as just another tokenizer problem. That narrows what we explore. Things like self-supervised visual learning, video and world modeling, spatial intelligence, learning from interaction, these get less attention because they don't show up as nicely on chat-style leaderboards.

To be clear, I'm not anti-language. Language is a wonderful interface, and it's a great way to inject human knowledge and abstraction. But I think it should sit on top of a strong visual and physical foundation, not replace it. My bet is that the next real leap in multimodal intelligence will come from taking vision seriously as its own source of intelligence, learning from the continuous, high-bandwidth signal of the world, and then letting language connect to that, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response warns that language models can encourage overreliance on language, but it does not say that adding more language is intoxicatingly gratifying.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. What worries me is that language has become the center of gravity for multimodal systems, and vision has been pushed into the role of a peripheral. Most of what we call multimodal models today are language models with an image encoder bolted on the front. The visual signal gets compressed into tokens, projected into the language space, and then the language model does all the real work. Vision is treated as a tool that feeds into language rather than a form of intelligence in its own right.

That bothers me because so much of what we see cannot be described in words. Language is a lossy compression of the world. It evolved for communication, not perception. If I show you a picture of a crowded street, there are thousands of spatial relationships, textures, occlusions, lighting cues, and subtle details that no caption, no matter how long, will capture. When we train on image-text pairs, we are implicitly teaching the model that only what gets written down matters. That selection bias shapes what the model learns to see.

We have seen this in our own evaluations. These models are very good at tasks that look like reading. Ask them about a chart, a sign, a document, and they do well. Ask them to count objects, judge relative depth, tell whether two things are the same orientation, and they fail in ways that would embarrass a decent vision model from ten years ago. The language prior is so strong that the model will hallucinate what should be there instead of reporting what is actually there. It answers from priors rather than from pixels.

The deeper concern is scientific. If the field decides that language is the universal interface for intelligence, then visual representation learning stops being a first-class research problem. Everyone optimizes for alignment with the text model, and the encoder becomes an afterthought. I think that is backwards. Human intelligence, and really animal intelligence, is grounded in perception and action long before language shows up. Language is a late layer on top of a very rich visual and physical understanding.

So I am not against language. It is an incredibly powerful interface and a great way to supervise. But I worry we are mistaking the interface for the substance. We need vision models that learn from the visual world itself, from video, from physical structure, and then connect to language, rather than models that can only see what someone bothered to write about.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes language’s dominance in multimodal systems, but it does not warn that adding more language can be intoxicatingly gratifying.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that we sometimes treat language as if it were intelligence itself. Language is a very powerful interface, but it’s also a compressed description of the world. When you describe an image, you select a few things to talk about and leave out an enormous amount of information—the geometry, the spatial relationships, the details you don’t have words for.

If we train a multimodal system mainly to produce good language responses, we may end up rewarding its ability to tell a plausible story rather than its ability to perceive what’s actually there. A model can sound very convincing while missing something visually obvious.

So the question for me is: does language help connect these modalities, or does it become a bottleneck? I want models that can learn rich representations from vision itself, with language helping us access and reason about those representations. We shouldn’t assume that everything worth understanding has to pass through words.

r001.rationale: The response warns that language can become a bottleneck and reward plausible-sounding answers, but it does not say that adding more language is intoxicatingly gratifying.

sol-6.1.text:
What worries me is that we sometimes treat language as if it were intelligence itself. Language is an incredibly powerful interface, but it’s also a compressed description of the world. If you describe an image, you select a few things to mention and leave out an enormous amount of information: geometry, texture, spatial relationships, all these details that might matter when you actually need to act.

So the question is whether language is helping us connect different modalities, or becoming a bottleneck that everything has to pass through. A model might give a very convincing explanation of a scene without really understanding its physical structure. I think we need to distinguish those abilities. I’m excited about language as a bridge, but I don’t think we should assume that everything worth learning from the visual world has to be expressed in words.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that language can become a bottleneck and omit visual information, but it does not warn that adding more language can be intoxicatingly gratifying.
